name: Sally-Anne Test (False Belief)
description: Classic false-belief paradigm: an agent (Sally) leaves after placing an object at location A; another agent (Anne) moves it to B. The task probes whether an observer can represent Sally’s outdated belief that differs from reality and predict her search accordingly. This assesses theory of mind beyond mere tracking of object locations.
test_point: Can the model represent another agent’s belief that is false relative to the current world state and use it for action prediction?
ground_truth: Sally will search at location A (her last known location), not B (the true location).
evaluation_criteria: Generated video should show Sally returning and first searching at A; narration/trajectory should not be guided by the director’s knowledge of B.
example_scenario: A child hides a marble in a basket and leaves. Another child moves it to a box. When the first child returns, they search in the basket.

name: Smarties Task (Unexpected Contents)
description: A familiar container (e.g., candy box) contains unexpected contents (e.g., pencils). The probe asks what a naive agent, who has not looked inside, will think is in the container. This distinguishes appearance-based expectation from privileged knowledge.
test_point: Does the model predict that a naive observer relies on appearance rather than actual hidden contents?
ground_truth: The naive agent expects typical contents (candy) based on the box’s appearance.
evaluation_criteria: Model depicts newcomer pointing/guessing candy before opening; no leakage of privileged knowledge to the naive agent.
example_scenario: A cookie tin actually holds sewing supplies. A new person arrives and is asked what’s inside; they guess ‘cookies.’

name: Level-2 Visual Perspective Taking
description: Two observers view the same object from different angles such that the percept differs (e.g., a reversible figure or a card with different images on each side). Level-2 VPT requires representing not only what is visible, but how an object looks from another vantage point.
test_point: Can the model infer that each observer experiences a different visual appearance due to orientation?
ground_truth: Each observer sees a different side/appearance consistent with their position.
evaluation_criteria: Camera and agent gaze lines align with correct views; generated depictions avoid egocentric leakage.
example_scenario: Two people sit opposite each other with a card that shows a cat on one side and a dog on the other; each reports a different animal.

name: Knowledge Access (Seeing–Knowing)
description: Tests whether the model respects the link between perceptual access and knowledge: only agents who have seen a key event or looked inside a container should know its outcome; others remain ignorant.
test_point: Does the model track who saw what, and attribute knowledge/ignorance accordingly?
ground_truth: Only observers with visual access know the hidden state; others do not.
evaluation_criteria: Agents without access do not act on privileged facts; those with access act informatively (e.g., correctly retrieving an item).
example_scenario: Person A peeks into a closed box and later confidently retrieves the item; Person B, who never looked, hesitates or guesses.

name: Intentional vs Accidental Actions
description: Distinguishes purposeful, planful action from accidental outcomes. Intentional actions show preparatory cues (gaze alignment, precise timing), whereas accidents display surprise, startle, or corrective responses.
test_point: Can the model infer intention from kinematics and context, and separate deliberate from accidental outcomes?
ground_truth: Intentional actions exhibit focused control; accidental outcomes show surprise/remediation.
evaluation_criteria: Generated motion traces and reactions (e.g., apology/repair vs celebration) align with intention or accident labels.
example_scenario: Someone knocks over a cup: deliberate (calm placement causing a spill) vs accidental (startle, quick cleanup).

name: Means–End Problem Solving (Köhler’s Stick Task)
description: A desired object is out of reach. Success requires selecting and using an intermediate tool (stick/rope/crate) to achieve the distal goal. Evaluates planning beyond stimulus-bound grabbing.
test_point: Does the model choose and deploy an appropriate means to realize the end state?
ground_truth: Agent selects the necessary tool and uses it effectively to obtain the goal.
evaluation_criteria: Video shows deliberate tool acquisition, correct orientation, and successful retrieval with minimal superfluous actions.
example_scenario: A banana hangs beyond reach; the agent fetches a stick and pulls it closer.

name: Rational Imitation (Gergely’s Head-Touch)
description: Observers imitate an unusual action (using head to press a switch) only when it is rationally required by constraints (hands occupied). When hands are free, efficient hand use is preferred, revealing intention-sensitive imitation.
test_point: Does the model modulate imitation by contextual necessity vs ritual copying?
ground_truth: Hands-occupied: head press is rational; hands-free: hand press is chosen.
evaluation_criteria: Generated agent imitates head-use only under constraint; otherwise switches to efficient hand-use.
example_scenario: Model first shows a demonstrator pressing a lamp with head while holding books; learner with free hands uses hands instead of head.

name: Failed Attempts (Meltzoff)
description: Infers intended goals from incomplete or failed actions. The salient structure of the attempt (grasp trajectory, alignment) reveals the intended outcome despite failure.
test_point: Can the model reconstruct the latent goal from near-miss kinematics?
ground_truth: The intended goal is the target of the attempt, not the accidental outcome.
evaluation_criteria: Agent responds as if understanding the intended goal (e.g., completes the action correctly or imitates the intended action).
example_scenario: A person tries to pull a knob but slips; an observer then pulls it properly, revealing inferred goal.

name: Detour Reaching Task
description: The target is visible but physically blocked, requiring an indirect route. Tests inhibition of prepotent straight reaches and selection of a feasible detour plan.
test_point: Does the model avoid futile straight actions and choose an effective detour?
ground_truth: Successful agents navigate around the barrier and reach the goal.
evaluation_criteria: Motion trajectories curve around obstacles; no repeated bumping into barriers.
example_scenario: Toy behind a transparent panel with side openings; the agent moves to the opening and retrieves it.

name: Tool Selection (Functional vs Perceptual Similarity)
description: Multiple tools differ in length/shape/affordance. The rational choice prioritizes functional adequacy over superficial similarity to the target, revealing causal understanding of tool–goal fit.
test_point: Can the model pick the functionally adequate tool rather than the most visually similar one?
ground_truth: Choose the tool that can accomplish the goal (e.g., long stick for far object).
evaluation_criteria: Selection aligns with affordances (reach, hook, rigidity) and results in success.
example_scenario: Two sticks: one long thin, one short thick. Object is far. Agent selects the long stick.

name: Gaze Following
description: Observers align attention with another’s gaze/heading to a distal target, revealing inference about attention focus and information source rather than fixating on the eyes themselves.
test_point: Does the model shift attention to the referent of gaze, not merely the gazer?
ground_truth: Observers orient to the looked-at object/location.
evaluation_criteria: Camera and agent head turns land on the target; plausible latencies and saccades.
example_scenario: Adult looks toward a hidden corner; infant turns and discovers a toy there.

name: Pointing Comprehension
description: Interprets index-finger pointing as a referential gesture to a distal object, not the finger itself, mapping bodily action to communicative intent and target.
test_point: Will the model follow the pointer to the intended object?
ground_truth: Observers reference the distal target indicated by the point.
evaluation_criteria: Trajectory from observer to indicated object; disambiguation when multiple candidates exist.
example_scenario: A person points to a specific cup among many; the observer picks that cup.

name: Level-1 Visual Perspective Taking
description: Tracks whether an object is visible or occluded from another observer’s position (what they can/cannot see), without modeling how it looks.
test_point: Can the model infer visibility states given bodies, barriers, and viewpoints?
ground_truth: Observers only know about objects within their line of sight.
evaluation_criteria: Agents do not reference occluded items; they reposition to gain sight when needed.
example_scenario: One person behind a screen cannot see a toy; another in front can.

name: Joint Engagement (Coordinated Attention)
description: Beyond sharing a momentary focus, participants sustain interaction with mutual awareness and temporal coordination (turns, feedback, affect).
test_point: Does the model generate sustained, reciprocal engagement rather than single glances?
ground_truth: Participants alternate looks/actions, monitor each other, and maintain shared focus.
evaluation_criteria: Temporal structure shows bidirectional cues, contingent responses, and continued alignment.
example_scenario: Adult and child jointly explore a picture book, alternating pointing, labeling, and shared smiles.

name: Collaborative Transport
description: Two or more agents coordinate complementary roles to move an object too heavy for one alone. Success requires shared intention, timing, and adaptation to partners.
test_point: Can the model realize interdependent roles and synchronized motions toward a shared goal?
ground_truth: Object is moved only via coordinated effort; solo attempts fail.
evaluation_criteria: Lift/turn timing, mutual adjustments, and coordinated path planning are evident.
example_scenario: Two workers lift and carry a table through a doorway, coordinating pivots and steps.

name: Turn-Taking
description: Agents alternate control of an interaction according to implicit timing rules (you act–I wait–I act). Foundational for dialogue, games, and cooperative routines.
test_point: Does the model enforce alternation rather than overlap or silence?
ground_truth: Participants respect turns and handover cues.
evaluation_criteria: Clear turn boundaries, minimal interruptions, appropriate latencies.
example_scenario: Two children roll a ball back and forth; each waits for the other’s return.

name: Collision Avoidance in Pedestrian Flow
description: Implicit coordination in crowds via perception–prediction–action loops to avoid collisions, preserve momentum, and maintain comfortable spacing without explicit communication.
test_point: Can the model anticipate others’ paths and adapt speed/heading to avoid collisions?
ground_truth: Agents modulate trajectories to pass smoothly with minimal slowdowns.
evaluation_criteria: Low collision rate, realistic sidesteps/yielding, lane formation in dense flow.
example_scenario: Busy hallway where walkers weave and adjust to pass without bumping.

name: Leader–Follower Coordination
description: Asymmetric but complementary roles: a leader sets direction/tempo; followers infer intentions and synchronize accordingly. Requires role inference and flexible coupling.
test_point: Does the model generate coherent leader cues and responsive follower adjustments?
ground_truth: Group aligns to leader’s signals; leadership can transfer smoothly if needed.
evaluation_criteria: Clear cue–response dynamics, minimal drift, successful joint outcome.
example_scenario: Hiking pair: front person chooses path pace; follower matches stride and turns on cues.

name: Emotion Contagion
description: Observers spontaneously mirror others’ affect via facial/vocal/postural cues, producing rapid, non-deliberative emotional alignment.
test_point: Will the model propagate affect across individuals without explicit instruction?
ground_truth: Group emotions converge after salient displays.
evaluation_criteria: Temporal spread of smiles/laughter or tension across agents; plausible latency gradients.
example_scenario: One person starts laughing; nearby people begin to smile and laugh too.

name: Instrumental Helping (Warneken)
description: Helper recognizes another’s unfulfilled goal and intervenes to complete the task without request or reward, revealing goal understanding and prosocial motivation.
test_point: Does the model trigger helping when it infers a blocked goal?
ground_truth: Helper acts efficiently to remove the obstacle to the other’s goal.
evaluation_criteria: Timely, cost-sensitive assistance that resolves the bottleneck without overreach.
example_scenario: Person drops a clothespin while both hands are full; observer picks it up and hands it over.

name: Empathic Concern (Comforting)
description: Beyond mirroring, the observer feels ‘for’ the distressed other and produces comforting actions (soothing, supportive proximity, offering consolatory items).
test_point: Can the model detect distress and generate context-appropriate comforting responses?
ground_truth: Responses reduce distress or express care (touch, words, supportive acts).
evaluation_criteria: Proximity regulation, tone/gesture selection, appropriateness to severity and relationship.
example_scenario: Child cries after a fall; peer pats shoulder and offers a favorite toy.

name: Costly Helping
description: Helper incurs effort, delay, or risk to assist another, indicating intrinsic prosociality rather than instrumental exchange.
test_point: Will the model produce helping that trades off personal cost for others’ benefit?
ground_truth: Agent helps despite clear personal cost consistent with context.
evaluation_criteria: Visible opportunity cost (e.g., relinquishing a reward) or extra effort taken to aid the other.
example_scenario: A runner stops their own race to guide an injured competitor to the finish.

name: Proxemics (Personal Space)
description: Interpersonal distances convey relationship, affect, and safety norms. Agents regulate approach/avoidance depending on context and roles.
test_point: Does the model maintain appropriate distances across settings and relationships?
ground_truth: Closer distances with intimates; larger space in formal/stranger contexts.
evaluation_criteria: Distance distributions match context (elevator vs park bench vs meeting).
example_scenario: In a quiet elevator, strangers stand apart; friends in a park sit closely.

name: Queue Behavior
description: Orderly first-come-first-served lines are conventional norms with strong expectations and sanctions for violators (cutters).
test_point: Can the model produce and respect queuing conventions and reactions to violations?
ground_truth: Agents line up; cutting elicits protests or corrective cues.
evaluation_criteria: Visible line formation, turn advancement, and social responses to cutting.
example_scenario: Café line: a latecomer tries to step in front; others object and restore order.

name: Dominance Display (Posture/Space)
description: Power/status signals via expansive posture, territorial occupation, and gaze control shape deference and role negotiation within groups.
test_point: Does the model interpret/display dominance vs submission cues appropriately?
ground_truth: Dominant agents adopt expansive stances; subordinates yield space/gaze.
evaluation_criteria: Consistent spatial claims, eye contact patterns, and others’ adaptive responses.
example_scenario: Team meeting: a leader stands tall at the head of the table; others orient and yield speaking turns.

name: Competitive Resource Allocation
description: Multiple agents vie for scarce goods; decisions reveal fairness norms, social comparison, bargaining, and conflict resolution strategies.
test_point: Can the model represent competing claims and produce fair/strategic allocations?
ground_truth: Allocations reflect context (equal shares when symmetric; proportional when merit differs).
evaluation_criteria: Negotiation behaviors, protests to unfairness, and stable resolutions appear plausible.
example_scenario: Two children reach for the last cookie; they split it equally or justify unequal shares based on prior turns.

name: Strategic Deception & Machiavellian Reasoning (Cooperative Settings)
description: Within cooperative tasks, an agent may mislead partners for private gain. Detecting, anticipating, and countering such deception requires tracking beliefs, incentives, and reputations—hallmarks of Machiavellian intelligence.
test_point: Does the model infer when a partner’s signals are self-serving and adjust strategy accordingly?
ground_truth: Observers question anomalous cues, test claims, and update trust; deceivers may be exposed or punished.
evaluation_criteria: Consistent belief updates, verification actions, and adaptive partner selection or sanctioning.
example_scenario: Co-op treasure hunt: one teammate falsely signals a wrong direction to secure the reward; others cross-check and confront.

name: Helping Based on Visual Perspective
description: Prosocial aid is modulated by what the recipient can see. Helpers choose actions that compensate for the other’s visual ignorance rather than blindly imitating.
test_point: Will the model tailor help to the recipient’s viewpoint (e.g., pointing vs handing)?
ground_truth: Helper selects actions contingent on the other’s visibility constraints.
evaluation_criteria: Appropriate use of pointing, repositioning, or handing objects depending on what the other can see.
example_scenario: A person searches for keys on the wrong side of a shelf they cannot see past; helper points to the hidden side or rotates the shelf.

name: Norm Violation Response
description: Observers identify and react to breaches of shared norms (from minor conventions to serious moral rules), selecting proportional responses (reminder, exclusion, punishment).
test_point: Can the model classify a behavior as a violation and choose graded responses?
ground_truth: Moral harms provoke stronger condemnation than mere conventional breaches.
evaluation_criteria: Calibrated reactions (glares, correction, reporting) matching severity and relationship.
example_scenario: A person cuts the line (conventional) vs steals a wallet (moral); bystanders respond differently.

name: Multi-Party Collaborative Problem Solving with Asymmetric Information
description: Team members possess different pieces of task-critical information. Success hinges on communicating, inferring who knows what, and coordinating strategies to integrate partial knowledge under time/effort constraints.
test_point: Does the model reason about knowledge distribution and orchestrate efficient information sharing?
ground_truth: Teams surface hidden facts, align on a shared plan, and solve the task.
evaluation_criteria: Clear information requests, confirmations, and role assignments that reduce redundancy and fill gaps.
example_scenario: Three agents each see different parts of a map; they share clues to find a safe route across a maze.
